title: Who Really Made Alexander "the Great"? #history #shorts
description:
Who really made Alexander "the Great"? Alexander wept: no worlds left to conquer... or did he?

Son of Zeus, the horse no one could ride, the Gordian knot cut with a sword, an empire from Greece to India and not one battle lost. Or so the story goes. The battles are real: Issus, Gaugamela, the Hydaspes. But Plutarch tells it differently: a philosopher told Alexander there were infinite worlds, and he wept because he had not conquered even one. And no text from his lifetime calls him "the Great". Most of those writings are lost, and the earliest use we have is a Roman comedy, Plautus' Mostellaria, about 200 BC (probably adapted from a Greek play). If the worlds are infinite... can anyone ever be great?

Sources: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 2-6 and On Tranquility of Mind 466D; Arrian, Anabasis 2.3; Plautus, Mostellaria 775 (c. 200 BC).
Pictures: Alexander Mosaic, House of the Faun, Pompeii, a Roman copy (c. 100 BC) of a Hellenistic painting (photo TyB, CC BY 2.0); André Castaigne, The Taming of Bucephalus (1898); Alexander Cutting the Gordian Knot, 18th-century French (Wikimedia Commons); head of a philosopher, perhaps Plutarch, Archaeological Museum of Delphi (public domain). Map drawn from Natural Earth data (public domain).
